newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: KLM IN RADIOACTIVE FREIGHT SCARE.
newsitem.headline: KLM IN RADIOACTIVE FREIGHT SCARE.

text.p: The Dutch transport ministry said on Sunday it was considering putting Dutch carrier KLM on probation after the airline allegedly flouted legal regulations on transporting radioactive materials.

A ministry spokesman said that KLM's failure to conduct the required inspection of a cargo of radioactive medical equipment submitted by a Dutch firm for shipment constituted a "serious violation" of legal procedures.
"The ministry is weighing the conditional withdrawal of KLM's permit to transport hazardous, particularly radioactive, materials," spokesman Henk Houtman said.
He said the case, which concerned a radioactive cargo carried on board KLM's May 2 KL129 passenger flight to London, was due to be heard on Tuesday.

The ministry would then decide whether to put KLM on probation for a period yet to be determined, during which time a second offence would lead to the carrier's permit being lastingly withdrawn, Houtman said.

The cargo was monitored on arrival in London during routine checks by Britain's Civil Aviation Authority and found to be emitting higher levels of radiation than those indicated in its freight documents, Houtman said.

He said the fault had started at the Petten-based company submitting the cargo for shipment, which had not packaged the equipment properly and had subsequently failed to measure the levels of radiation being emitted.
KLM in turn had not carried out the required acceptance checks, he said.
KLM's head of cargo Jacques Ancher told Dutch television in an interview that a preliminary probe into the affair had not shown the airline to be culpable.

"I think ...that retrospective investigations have shown that throughout the whole chain from departure to arrival a number of things went wrong... until now it has not become evident that (KLM) was at fault," Ancher said.
Ancher denied allegations that KLM had failed to notify the Dutch authorities of the higher-than-reported levels of radiation detected by the British inspectors.
He added, "according to our information we remained far below the (radiation safety) norms that have been set and we think therefore that there will be no effect."
But he added that the furore raised by the story, which broke in Britain's Observer newspaper early Sunday, had persuaded KLM to inform the passengers concerned.
"We have since decided because this has come up to inform the passengers and we will be doing so in the very near future," he said.
However, KLM's assurances of minimal radiation doses were countered by the transport ministry.

Spokesman Henk Houtman said a probe by Dutch health authorities indicated the level of radiation absorbed by passengers sitting directly over the cargo during the one-hour flight would have equalled the maximum annual dose considered safe.
"As such it becomes very difficult to say whether or not safety norms have been breached," he said.

Citing confidential documents, the Observer newspaper said the cargo had been stowed in the plane's hold just below the galley and rows six and seven, where mainly British and American passengers were seated.
